title: Stewardship and Judgment
overview: Luke 16 presents two profound teachings of Jesus focusing on stewardship, wealth, and eternal consequences. The chapter opens with the parable of the unjust steward, illustrating shrewdness in worldly affairs and urging believers to use earthly resources wisely for eternal benefit. Jesus then teaches about faithfulness in handling wealth, warning against serving two masters—God and mammon. The chapter concludes with the vivid account of the rich man and Lazarus, emphasizing the reality of judgment after death and the eternal reversal of fortunes based on earthly conduct. This chapter challenges believers to consider their priorities, faithfulness, and the eternal impact of their earthly lives within the broader message of the Gospel.
structure:
**Verses 1-8: The Parable of the Unjust Steward.** Jesus tells a story about a steward accused of wasting his master's goods, who cleverly reduces debts to secure favor after dismissal. The parable highlights wisdom in using worldly resources and the importance of shrewdness in spiritual matters.

**Verses 9-13: Teachings on Wealth and Faithfulness.** Jesus instructs His disciples to be faithful in managing worldly wealth, emphasizing that faithfulness in little leads to trust in much, and warns that no one can serve both God and mammon.

**Verses 14-18: Jesus’ Rebuke of the Pharisees and Teaching on the Law.** The covetous Pharisees mock Jesus, who responds by exposing their self-righteousness and affirming the enduring validity of the Law and the Prophets.

**Verses 19-31: The Story of the Rich Man and Lazarus.** A rich man living in luxury ignores the beggar Lazarus at his gate. After death, Lazarus is comforted in Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man suffers torment. The narrative underscores the consequences of earthly choices and the sufficiency of Scripture for repentance.

keyVerses.text: And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the commendation of worldly shrewdness, challenging believers to be equally wise in spiritual matters. It underscores the need for prudent stewardship of earthly resources with eternal perspective.

keyVerses.text: No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
keyVerses.significance: A foundational teaching on loyalty and devotion, this verse warns that divided allegiance between God and wealth is impossible, calling believers to wholehearted service to God alone.

keyVerses.text: There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day:
keyVerses.significance: This verse sets the scene for the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, illustrating earthly wealth and luxury that contrast starkly with spiritual poverty and eternal judgment.

keyVerses.text: But Abraham said, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.
keyVerses.significance: This verse teaches the principle of eternal recompense based on earthly life, affirming the reality of judgment and the reversal of fortunes after death.

keyVerses.text: And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.
keyVerses.significance: This verse emphasizes the sufficiency and authority of Scripture for repentance and salvation, underscoring that miraculous signs alone will not convince those who reject God's word.

characters.name: The Unjust Steward
characters.description: A manager accused of wasting his master's goods who acts shrewdly to secure his future. His actions illustrate worldly wisdom and serve as a lesson on using resources wisely for eternal purposes.

characters.name: The Rich Man
characters.description: A wealthy individual living in luxury who ignores the poor beggar Lazarus. His story serves as a warning about the dangers of selfishness and the consequences of neglecting others and God’s commands.

characters.name: Lazarus
characters.description: A poor beggar covered with sores who longs for crumbs from the rich man's table. After death, he is comforted in Abraham's bosom, symbolizing the blessed state of the righteous after death.

characters.name: Abraham
characters.description: The patriarch who appears in the parable as the figure of comfort for Lazarus and judge who explains the consequences of the rich man's choices, emphasizing the finality of judgment.

characters.name: The Pharisees
characters.description: Religious leaders who are covetous and mock Jesus’ teachings. They represent self-righteousness and hypocrisy, serving as a foil to Jesus’ message about true faithfulness and repentance.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes faithful and wise management of earthly resources, urging believers to use wealth to build eternal relationships and not to serve mammon.
Through the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, the chapter teaches that earthly riches do not guarantee eternal security and that neglecting the needy leads to eternal consequences.
Jesus teaches that faithfulness in small matters reflects one’s character and readiness for greater responsibilities, highlighting the importance of integrity in all areas of life.
The chapter affirms that the Law and the Prophets remain authoritative and sufficient for guiding repentance and faith, even in the face of miraculous signs.
The impossibility of serving both God and mammon underscores the call to undivided loyalty and wholehearted devotion to God alone.

historicalContext: Luke's Gospel was written in the first century AD, addressing a primarily Gentile audience familiar with Jewish customs and teachings. Stewardship was a common theme in the Greco-Roman world, where servants or stewards managed estates for wealthy masters. The parable reflects this social structure, illustrating practical wisdom expected in managing resources. The Pharisees, as religious leaders, were influential in Jewish society and often criticized by Jesus for hypocrisy and legalism. The story of the rich man and Lazarus reflects Jewish beliefs about the afterlife, resurrection, and the importance of the Law and Prophets, which were central to Jewish identity and ethics during this period.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes the sovereignty of God over all resources and the believer’s responsibility to steward wealth for God’s glory and the good of others. The parable of the unjust steward teaches prudence in using worldly means to secure eternal friendships, while the rich man’s fate underscores the necessity of repentance and faith.

Dispensationalists often see the parable as illustrating practical wisdom in the present age, with the rich man and Lazarus story emphasizing the reality of eternal judgment and the fixed nature of the afterlife. The sufficiency of Scripture for salvation is highlighted as a key point.

Early Church Fathers like Augustine interpreted the unjust steward as a symbol of the Christian’s use of worldly wealth to gain eternal rewards. The rich man and Lazarus parable was seen as a warning against greed and a call to charity, emphasizing the finality of judgment and the importance of heeding Scripture.

crossReferences.connection: Jesus’ teaching that no man can serve two masters parallels Luke 16:13, reinforcing the call to exclusive devotion to God over wealth.
This passage about honoring the Lord with wealth complements the stewardship theme in Luke 16, encouraging faithful management of resources.
Paul’s instructions to the rich to be generous and store up treasures in heaven echo the warnings and teachings of Luke 16 regarding wealth and eternal security.
The certainty of death and judgment in Hebrews supports the depiction of afterlife consequences in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus.
James’ teaching on faith and works aligns with the call in Luke 16 to demonstrate faithfulness through actions, especially toward the needy.

application: Evaluate your stewardship of resources and seek to use them wisely for eternal purposes.
Commit to serving God wholeheartedly, avoiding divided loyalties with wealth or materialism.
Practice faithfulness in small responsibilities as preparation for greater spiritual trust.
Respond to Scripture’s call to repentance, recognizing its sufficiency for salvation.
Show compassion and generosity to those in need, remembering the eternal consequences of neglect.
Trust in God’s justice and live with an eternal perspective on earthly life.
conclusion: Luke 16 challenges believers to reconsider their relationship with wealth, faithfulness, and eternal destiny. Through the parable of the unjust steward, Jesus calls for wise and faithful management of earthly resources, while the story of the rich man and Lazarus starkly warns of the consequences of selfishness and neglect. The chapter’s teachings on serving God alone and the enduring authority of Scripture remain vital for Christian living today, urging believers to live with integrity, compassion, and an eternal perspective.
timeline: c. AD 30-33 - Ministry of Jesus Christ in Galilee and Judea

definitions.definition: A person entrusted with managing another’s property or affairs, responsible for faithful administration.
A term used to describe wealth or material riches, often personified as a master competing with God for loyalty.
Something detestable or loathsome in the sight of God, often used to describe sinful attitudes or actions.
A small stroke or mark in Hebrew writing; used here to emphasize the unchanging nature of the Law down to the smallest detail.
A Jewish expression referring to the place of comfort in the afterlife where the righteous dead await resurrection.

outline.heading: The Parable of the Unjust Steward
outline.description: Jesus tells a story about a steward who, facing dismissal, shrewdly reduces debts owed to his master to secure future favor. The parable teaches the importance of wise use of worldly resources for eternal benefit.

outline.heading: Teachings on Wealth and Faithfulness
outline.description: Jesus instructs His followers to be faithful in managing worldly wealth, emphasizing that faithfulness in little leads to trust in much and warning against serving two masters.

outline.heading: Jesus’ Rebuke of the Pharisees and Affirmation of the Law
outline.description: Jesus confronts the covetous Pharisees who mock Him, exposing their hypocrisy and affirming the enduring validity of the Law and the Prophets.

outline.heading: The Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus
outline.description: A rich man lives in luxury while Lazarus suffers at his gate. After death, their fortunes are reversed, illustrating the reality of judgment and the sufficiency of Scripture for repentance.
